[SYSTEM]
You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: The query is glipizide, a sulfonylurea sharing the N-cyclohexylsulfonylurea and phenethyl linker with glyburide (L6 M03) and related to glimepiride (L6 M02) and tolbutamide (L6 M01); glyburide is the closest transferable experimental reference.

L4 glyburide Caco-2 absorptive permeability (Papp 18.1 ± 0.8 ×10^-6 cm/s) and passive permeability (19.0 ± 2.6 ×10^-6 cm/s) support efficient intestinal absorption for this chemotype despite ionization.

L3 oral-exposure records for sulfonylureas show substantial systemic AUC/Cmax after oral dosing (glyburide AUCss 525.7 ng·h/mL; glimepiride AUC0-∞ 1215 ng·h/mL; gliclazide AUC0-∞ 56.32 µg·h/mL), consistent with F≥20%.
L5 shows glyburide is a Pgp/BCRP/OATP2B1 substrate with efflux ratios 2.65–4, but in vivo jejunal efflux after IV is only 0.02–0.03% of dose in 60 min, so gut-wall efflux is not threshold-relevant.

L6 hepatic metabolism: glimepiride shows <5% turnover in liver microsomes and low hepatic clearance (2.1 L/h/1.73 m²); tolbutamide shows low CYP2C9 intrinsic clearance; glyburide shows higher HLM CLint (52.9–67.2 µL/min/mg) and fast CYP3A4 turnover, but these are intrinsic in vitro values without unbound-fraction/scaling and do not affirm F<20%.

No direct absolute F measurement for glipizide or a close sulfonylurea is supplied; the high prediction rests on transferable permeability, solubility, oral exposure, efflux, and metabolic evidence, so confidence remains moderate.

evidence_gaps: No direct absolute oral bioavailability measurement for glipizide or any sulfonylurea is supplied; F is inferred from permeability, solubility, oral exposure, efflux, and hepatic metabolism.
No matched oral-versus-IV comparison for glipizide or a close sulfonylurea analog is supplied.

No glipizide-specific Caco-2, solubility, dissolution, transporter, or hepatic metabolism data are supplied; transfer from glyburide/glimepiride/tolbutamide is based on the shared sulfonylurea core, but the benzamide/pyrazinecarboxamide difference could alter metabolism and transporter affinity.
L6 hepatic intrinsic clearance values for glyburide are not accompanied by unbound fraction or in vivo scaling, so their impact on F is uncertain.

Condition match is imperfect: the query has no reported external condition, while some training contexts are fed/fasted/cirrhosis; L3-L6 records are mostly healthy/fasted/fed and may not capture disease effects.
No ChEMBL evidence was provided; the physicochemical prior is uncertain and not used as endpoint proof.
content.decision_summary: Predicted high because the query is a glipizide-like sulfonylurea; L4 shows high Caco-2 permeability and adequate intestinal-fluid solubility/dissolution for glyburide, L3 shows substantial oral exposure for the sulfonylurea class, L5 shows gut-wall efflux is modest and in vivo jejunal secretion is small, and L6 hepatic intrinsic clearance values do not affirm F<20% (glimepiride/tolbutamide show low hepatic clearance; glyburide's high HLM CLint is not directly threshold-relevant). Confidence remains moderate because no direct F measurement for glipizide is supplied.

You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.
